answer:
The value of \(n^2+n+1\) modulo \(7\) depends only on \(n\bmod 7\). Checking the seven possible residues gives

\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
n\bmod 7&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\\ \hline
(n^2+n+1)\bmod 7&1&3&0&6&0&3&1
\end{array}
\]

Thus, we need \(n\equiv2\) or \(4\pmod7\).

Since \(1000=7\cdot142+6\), the first \(994\) integers contain \(142\) complete blocks of seven, contributing \(2\cdot142=284\) solutions. The remaining six integers have residues \(1,2,3,4,5,6\), contributing two more.

Therefore, the answer is \(\boxed{286}\).
